subject: physics
title: Equations of uniform acceleration and free fall
key_idea: When acceleration is constant, four equations link displacement s, initial velocity u, final velocity v, acceleration a and time t. They apply to free fall, where a is the acceleration of free fall g, about 9.81 m/s² downwards, when air resistance is ignored.

blocks.text: These equations apply only when acceleration is constant and motion is in a straight line. Each equation leaves out one of the five quantities.

items: Choose one direction as positive. Give every vector a sign.
Write down the quantities you know and the one you want.
Pick the equation that contains those four and leaves out the fifth.
Solving v² = u² + 2as gives a square root, so check the sign of v.

items.text: A car accelerates from rest at 2.5 m/s² for 8.0 s. Find its displacement.
u = 0, a = 2.5, t = 8.0, and s is wanted. Use s = ut + ½at².

diagram.alt: A slider showing how displacement and final velocity change with initial velocity, acceleration and time for uniform acceleration.

items: The four equations need constant acceleration in a straight line.
Pick the equation that leaves out the quantity you neither know nor want.
Give each vector a sign, using one direction as positive.

blocks.text: All four follow from the definitions of velocity and acceleration for constant acceleration.

items.text: a = (v − u) / t. Rearranging gives v = u + at.
With constant acceleration, the average velocity is ½(u + v).
s = average velocity × t, so s = ½(u + v)t. This is also the area under the v-t graph.
Put v = u + at into s = ½(u + v)t. This gives s = ut + ½at².
Substitute t = (v − u) / a into s = ½(u + v)t. This gives v² = u² + 2as.

items: v = u + at comes straight from the definition of acceleration.
s = ½(u + v)t comes from the area under the velocity-time graph.
The other two come from combining these.

blocks.text: In free fall the only force is weight. All objects then have the same acceleration, wherever their mass.

items.meaning: Motion under the force of gravity alone, with no air resistance.
The acceleration of free fall. Near the Earth's surface it is about 9.81 m/s², directed downwards.

items: Use a = g with the equations of motion. Take downwards as positive if the object falls.
For an object thrown upwards, take upwards as positive so a = −9.81 m/s².
At the highest point the velocity is momentarily zero, but the acceleration is still g.
Air resistance is ignored. It is small for dense, compact objects at low speed.

items.text: Hold a steel ball with an electromagnet at a measured height h above a trapdoor.
Switch the electromagnet off. This starts an electronic timer as the ball is released.
The ball hits the trapdoor, which opens a switch and stops the timer. Record the time t.
Repeat for a range of heights. Plot h against t² and find the gradient.
With u = 0, h = ½gt², so the gradient is ½g and g = 2 × gradient.

items: A light gate and timer can replace the trapdoor. A card of known width falling through the gate gives its velocity, and v² = 2gh gives g.
Use a large height to reduce the percentage uncertainty in h and t.
Take the mean of repeats at each height, and use a ball that is dense and small to limit air resistance.
Free fall has constant acceleration g ≈ 9.81 m/s² downwards.
Dropping a ball from rest gives h = ½gt², so a graph of h against t² has gradient ½g.

checks.q: A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 1.8 m. Calculate the time taken to reach the ground. Ignore air resistance. (g = 9.81 m/s²)
Derive v² = u² + 2as from v = u + at and s = ½(u + v)t.
checks.a: From the first, t = (v − u) / a. Substitute into the second: s = ½(u + v)(v − u) / a. So 2as = v² − u², giving v² = u² + 2as.

checks.q: A stone is thrown vertically upwards at 15 m/s. Calculate the greatest height reached. (g = 9.81 m/s²)
checks.a: At the top v = 0. Using v² = u² + 2as: 0 = 15² + 2 × (−9.81) × s, so s = 225 / 19.6 = 11 m.

items: Required practical 3 is the determination of g by a free-fall method, as described above.
The acceleration due to gravity is written g.
Apparatus may include trolleys, air-track gliders, ticker timers, light gates, data-loggers and video techniques.
A light gate records the time a card of known length takes to pass. Dividing length by time gives the velocity.
Two light gates, or one gate that records two times, give the acceleration.
An air track removes most friction, so the acceleration is close to constant.
For collisions, measure the velocities of each trolley or glider before and after.

items.meaning: The time between a driver seeing a hazard and applying the brakes.
The distance travelled during the reaction time, at constant speed.
The distance travelled while the brakes slow the vehicle to rest.

items: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time. It is directly proportional to speed.
Braking distance from v² = 2as is proportional to v² for a constant deceleration, so doubling speed quadruples it.
Reaction time rises with tiredness, alcohol, drugs and distraction.
Braking distance rises with a heavier load, worn tyres or brakes, and wet or icy roads, because the deceleration is smaller.
